title: They Sat in Silence for Seven Days… and Heaven Listened: The Forgotten Power of Sitting Shiva in Ancient Israel
paragraphs: They Sat in Silence for Seven Days… and Heaven Listened: The Forgotten Power of Sitting Shiva in Ancient Israel
When grief stripped away every word, God drew closest—not in noise, but in sacred silence.
There is a kind of pain that cannot be explained, only endured.
The kind that empties your chest, dries your tears, and leaves you staring at the ground because even heaven feels too far away to look up at.
Ancient Israel understood that kind of pain.
They didn’t rush it. They didn’t fix it. They didn’t preach over it.
They sat in it.
They called it something that still echoes today—Shiva.

From the Hebrew root שבע (shevaʿ), meaning “seven,” it was more than a number. It was completion. Fulfillment. A sacred cycle. When someone died, the family would enter into seven days of mourning—Shiv’ah—a time when life itself slowed down to honor loss, to face reality, and to allow grief to speak without interruption.
But what most people don’t realize is this wasn’t just a cultural practice.
It was deeply biblical.
And it reveals something about God that many have forgotten.
In Job 2:13, after everything was taken from Job—his children, his wealth, his health—his friends came to him. Not with answers. Not with theology. Not with motivational words.
They sat.
“וַיֵּשְׁבוּ אִתּוֹ לָאָרֶץ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים וְשִׁבְעַת לֵילוֹת וְאֵין דֹּבֵר אֵלָיו דָּבָר”
Vayeshevu itto la’aretz shiv’at yamim v’shiv’at leilot, v’ein dover elav davar.
“They sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him.”
No one spoke.
Because sometimes the holiest thing you can offer is not a voice—but your presence.
And maybe that’s where this is starting to hit you.
Because you’ve been surrounded by noise.
Advice. Opinions. Quick fixes. Shallow encouragement.
But your soul didn’t need noise.
It needed someone to sit with you.
To acknowledge the weight.
To not rush your healing.
To not demand your smile.
To not force your faith into performance.
And yet… even in ancient Israel, even in the sacred act of Shiva, there was something deeper happening beneath the silence.
Because silence was never the end.
It was the doorway.
You see, the Hebrew understanding of mourning wasn’t just about loss—it was about truth. It forced the mourner to face reality without distraction. No work. No entertainment. No pretending.
Just you…
and what’s broken.
And this is where it becomes uncomfortable.
Because many of us are not grieving death.
We’re grieving things we refuse to name.
Broken relationships.
Hidden sin.
Unspoken regrets.
The version of ourselves we know we’re supposed to be… but aren’t.
And instead of sitting in that truth, we run.
We scroll.
We distract.
We numb.
But ancient Israel would have told you something we don’t like to hear:
If you don’t sit in your grief… you will never meet God in it.
Because God does not rush what He intends to heal.
In the Greek New Testament, when Jesus approached grief, He didn’t bypass it either.
In John 11:35, standing before the tomb of Lazarus, knowing full well He was about to raise him, Jesus still wept.
“ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (edakrysen ho Iēsous)”
“Jesus wept.”
Not performed. Not pretended.
He wept.
Because grief matters to God.
Your pain is not an interruption to His plan.
It’s often the place where His presence becomes undeniable.
And yet here’s the scandal…
The same silence that reveals pain also exposes sin.
Because when everything is stripped away—when you finally stop running—you begin to hear something else.
Conviction.
The quiet whisper that says… something isn’t right.
The places you compromised.
The moments you chose darkness over light.
The habits you justified.
The distance you created between you and God.
And suddenly, Shiva becomes more than mourning loss.
It becomes confrontation.
Not from a God who wants to condemn you…
But from a God who refuses to leave you in what’s killing you.
Because the story doesn’t end in silence.
It never does.
It always moves toward redemption.
In Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke daily, the word for repentance carries depth beyond apology. It’s a turning. A returning.
And this is where everything changes.
Because what ancient Israel practiced externally…
Jesus fulfilled internally.
He stepped into our grief.
Our sin.
Our brokenness.
And instead of sitting beside it—He carried it.
“כִּי הוּא נָשָׂא חֳלָיֵנוּ (ki hu nasa cholayenu)” — Isaiah 53:4
“Surely He has borne our griefs.”
Not observed them.
Not analyzed them.
He bore them.
That means the silence you’ve been sitting in?
He’s already been there.
The guilt you don’t talk about?
He already carried it.
The version of you that feels too far gone?
He already paid for it.
And now the question isn’t whether God sees you.
It’s whether you’re ready to stop hiding from Him.
Because here’s the truth most people avoid:
You cannot experience resurrection if you refuse to acknowledge death.
You cannot receive grace if you won’t confront sin.
You cannot be healed if you won’t sit in what’s broken.
Shiva was never about staying in sorrow.
It was about preparing the heart for restoration.
And Jesus is the fulfillment of that restoration.
This is where the story turns.
Because grace doesn’t arrive when you pretend you’re okay.
It arrives when you admit you’re not.
And maybe that’s why you’re still reading this.
Because something in you knows…
You’ve been avoiding the silence.
Avoiding the truth.
Avoiding God.
But He hasn’t avoided you.
He’s been sitting there the whole time.
Waiting.
Not to shame you.
Not to expose you publicly.
But to bring you back to life.
So be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected, didn’t it?
Because silence is where transformation begins.
And if you’re serious about going deeper—not just feeling something, but actually growing in Christ—stay close.
Follow.
Because this isn’t about content.
This is about transformation.
And if you truly want to glorify God, don’t just consume truth—support the mission that spreads it.
This is not about money.
It’s about mission.
It’s about making sure truth keeps reaching the ones still sitting in silence.
Because someone out there is still in their Shiva moment…
And they need to know resurrection is coming.
You were never meant to stay in the silence… only to meet God there.
